[OpenPFC / Start learning]{.lesson-kicker}

# Six experiments. One equation you can understand.

[Give a grid physical meaning, put a field on it, and follow heat as it spreads. Then change the numerical method and explain what changes in the answer.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

Beginner · six lessons · allow about 45 minutes after setting up your SDK.
All six experiments run on one CPU process. Basic C++ loops and functions
are enough to start; each chapter explains the OpenPFC objects it introduces.

## Get ready once

Install the [OpenPFC SDK and native CLI](https://vtt-propertune.github.io/OpenPFC/docs/project/install/)
and load its compiler/MPI environment. These examples include Fourier
transforms, so choose an SDK with the CPU FFT/HeFFTe backend. Check it once:

```sh
openpfc doctor
```

Each lesson has a **Download runnable lesson** link. Extract the archive,
open its named folder, and use the command in its README. The package includes
the model, inputs and shared headers in their original relative layout.
The same C++ is shown in the chapter.

Recorded runs print an `Attempt` directory. Read its `stdout.log` for console
output and its `results/` directory for data files. Each run keeps its own
result, so you can compare experiments after changing an input.

## Take one step at a time

::: {.lesson-steps}
::: {.lesson-step}
[01 / Geometry]{.lesson-kicker}

### [Give the grid a physical meaning](../geometry/first-domain/index.qmd)

An index becomes a position through an origin and a spacing. Predict the
coordinate before running the short program.

**Check:** explain why the last periodic sample and the box's upper boundary
are different positions.
:::
::: {.lesson-step}
[02 / Fields]{.lesson-kicker}

### [Put values on that geometry](../geometry/field-storage/index.qmd)

A field connects physical coordinates, owned samples and memory. See the
same polynomial stored with and without halo padding.

**Check:** explain how 96 owned values can occupy either 96 or 288 slots.
:::
::: {.lesson-step}
[03 / Differentiation]{.lesson-kicker}

### [Compare three derivatives](../differentiation/periodic/index.qmd)

Apply second-order differences, fourth-order differences and Fourier
differentiation to the same smooth periodic function.

**Check:** find refinement ratios approaching four and sixteen, and identify
where floating-point roundoff stops further improvement.
:::
::: {.lesson-step}
[04 / Neighbouring values]{.lesson-kicker}

### [Let heat flow between samples](../heat/finite-differences/index.qmd)

Use neighbouring values to approximate a Laplacian, then advance the heat
equation with forward Euler. Read the update directly in C++.

**Check:** the mean stays near one while the temperature variation decreases.
Respect the chapter's explicit timestep bound when refining the grid.
:::
::: {.lesson-step}
[05 / Fourier modes]{.lesson-kicker}

### [Change the spatial derivative](../heat/fourier/index.qmd)

Keep the same equation, initial condition and Euler step. Compute the
Laplacian through Fourier coefficients instead.

**Check:** identify the time error that remains after this spatial change.
:::
::: {.lesson-step}
[06 / Exact evolution]{.lesson-kicker}

### [Let each wave decay exactly](../heat/exponential/index.qmd)

Solve the scalar equation of each retained Fourier mode with an exponential.
Compare the result with both earlier heat implementations.

**Check:** distinguish the continuum solution, the discrete spatial operator
and the time integration rule.
:::
:::

## Make a prediction, then test it

The three heat lessons use the same starting inputs and the same periodic
equation. Their initial field is

$$
u(x,y,z,0)=1+0.2\cos x\cos y\cos z,
$$

and the heat equation $u_t=D\nabla^2u$ gives

$$
u(x,y,z,t)=1+0.2e^{-3Dt}\cos x\cos y\cos z.
$$

Run each implementation with the supplied input. Open the final row of
`results/diagnostics.csv` in the printed attempt directory. Compare `mean`,
`rms_fluctuation` and `rms_error`.

Now halve `dt` and double `steps`, keeping the same final time. For the
starting case, the changed input is:

```json
{
  "n": 16,
  "steps": 200,
  "dt": 0.0005,
  "diffusivity": 1.0
}
```

Before running again, predict which error will decrease and which method
already has an exact evolution rule for this linear problem.

<details class="lesson-answer">
<summary>Check your prediction</summary>

The final time stays $T=0.1$. The mean remains one and the exact cosine
amplitude is $0.2e^{-0.3}\approx0.14816$.

For the Fourier/Euler model, the spatial representation resolves this mode;
Euler's first-order time error should decrease by about a factor of two.
For the exponential model, the retained modes already follow their exact
linear evolution, so a smaller timestep need not improve a result near
roundoff.

The finite-difference model has both spatial and time errors. They can
partly cancel, so its total error need not fall monotonically when only
the timestep changes. Keep the grid fixed to study time error, then use the
chapter's stability bound when refining space.

</details>
